sections.h2: Colorado Springs and your tax bill
sections.html:
Sitting below Pikes Peak roughly 70 miles south of Denver, Colorado Springs serves as the county seat of El Paso County. At 195.761 square miles it covers more ground than any other Colorado municipality, and that sprawl shows up on tax bills. A house against the western foothills and a new build on the far east side can land in different school, fire and metro districts, so two homes of equal value can owe different amounts. Homes range from historic districts, a legacy of the town's June 19, 1886 incorporation, to brand new subdivisions.

You will never get a bill from City Hall. The county treasurer's office does the billing and collecting for the city and every other taxing body.

sections.h2: Mill levies on a Colorado Springs bill
sections.html:
One mill means $1 of tax per $1,000 of assessed value, and your bill adds up every levy on the parcel. Colorado Springs itself levies 3.009 mills for tax year 2025 (billed in 2026), a drop from 3.554. Other entities, with the prior year for comparison:

  • El Paso County: 6.857 mills, against 6.985.
  • Pikes Peak Library District: 2.938, against 3.140.
  • Colorado Springs Downtown Development Authority: 5 in both years.

Schools take the biggest bite on most bills, and each district sets its own rate separately from other local governments. Tax year 2025 levies:

  • Colorado Springs School District 11: 37.695 mills.
  • Harrison School District 2: 39.989.
  • Academy School District 20: 45.459.
  • El Paso County School District 49: 45.649.
  • Widefield School District 3: 57.682.
  • Fountain-Fort Carson School District 8: 29.765.

The 2026 residential assessment rate for schools is 7.05%. Look at the district named on your statement before you compare your house with a neighbor's across a district line.

sections.h2: Fire, metro and other special districts
sections.html:
Some parcels carry extra levies for fire protection, improvements or a metro district. A few examples for tax year 2025:

  • Broadmoor Fire Protection District: 4.5 mills.
  • Black Forest Fire Protection District: 15.65 mills.
  • Old Colorado City Security and Maintenance District: 13.416 mills.
  • Banning Lewis Ranch Metro District No. 2: 46.469 mills, with neighboring districts at other levels.

Metro districts pay for roads, water and parks in newer subdivisions, and their levies run far above what a city or county charges. Owners in one can see its charge as a separate line, and buyers will ask about it.

The county's yearly calendar is below. A due date landing on a weekend or holiday slides to the following business day.

DateWhat happens
January 10Assessor hands the prior year's tax warrant to the Treasurer
January 28Deadline for mailing statements
Last day of FebruaryFirst half comes due
March 31Senior tax deferral applications due to the State Treasurer
April 30Whole-year payment comes due
June 15Second half comes due; anything unpaid turns delinquent
JulyDelinquency notices go out and interest begins
SeptemberOverdue real estate taxes are advertised ahead of the auction
After September 30Only cash or certified funds accepted
OctoberLiens on overdue real estate taxes are auctioned

Interest on a late bill runs 1% a month. There's no grace period, and the county won't take partial payments. The auction happens online through RealAuction, and bidders register at the end of September.

How you pay affects whether you are on time, so choose early.

  • Online: current-year taxes through the Property Tax Search and Payment Portal, by credit, debit or ACH.
  • In person: credit or debit card at the office, with card processing fees passed to the cardholder.
  • Mail: current-year payments count as timely with a USPS postmark dated by the due date. A postage meter stamp from your own office won't do.
  • Fixed income: owners can enroll in monthly payments through EscrowTaxes.
  • Tax liens and redemptions: pay with cash, a cashier's check or a money order. A postmark won't save a late one.

Cards stop being accepted for current-year taxes after September 30. The statement is mailed to the owner of record rather than the lender, so if you have a mortgage, ask whether the lender holds your taxes in escrow.

Call first. The County Assessor (1675 West Garden of the Gods Road, Suite 2300) wants an informal talk before any formal appeal, and the number is (719) 520-6600.

When a call doesn't settle it, the Board of Equalization is next, reached through the Clerk to the Board in Suite 2201 down the hall, (719) 520-6430. Protests on real property must reach the Board by July 15. Teams hearings fill July 6 through August 5. You and the county each present for 10 minutes, the burden of proving value sits with you, and the written ruling follows within five business days.

  • Your evidence must be market data dated January 1, 2023 through June 30, 2024, the window behind the 2025 and 2026 values.
  • Beyond the Board you can choose the Board of Assessment Appeals, district court or arbitration, filed inside 30 days of the ruling.
  • Court filings go to the Fourth Judicial District Court, 270 S. Tejon Street.

Binding arbitration through the county is final and cannot be reviewed.

A senior exemption exists when the state pays for it. It can erase up to 50% of the first $200,000 of a primary residence's value, and lawmakers restored funding for tax year 2026, payable in 2027.

First-time applicants need to be 65 by January 1, and to have owned and occupied the home for a minimum of 10 consecutive years. Surviving spouses use a different route. The application deadline moves, so call (719) 520-6600 for the current date. Colorado also offers a senior deferral. Think of it as a state treasurer loan, recorded as a lien and accruing interest from May 1. Selling the home or transferring title makes it payable.

Owing tax doesn't stop a sale. The typical sequence:

  1. Title staff request the payoff figure from the County Treasurer.
  2. Back tax and interest show as a payoff line and are subtracted from what you receive.
  3. A recorded deferral gets paid off too, because selling ends it.
  4. Once an account has been auctioned, the lien buyer's payoff is added to the tax.

Expect the title company to record the deed once funds clear. If you inherited the house or can't find old statements, the County Treasurer's portal lets you look up the parcel and see what is owed before you list.

Have your latest statement handy, with your school and any metro district named, when you first talk to the title officer. Anyone relocating or behind on a bill can also ask about an as-is cash sale, which skips repairs and showings. Owners near the western hills should check insurance and defensible space before listing, since the Waldo Canyon Fire of June 2012 destroyed 347 homes and buyers remember it.

faqs.q: Who bills property tax in Colorado Springs?
faqs.a: The county treasurer, not the city. Colorado Springs sets a 3.009 mill levy for tax year 2025, yet El Paso County sends the statement and collects for all districts.

faqs.q: What is the interest rate on late Colorado Springs property tax?
faqs.a: One percent per month, starting right away. Partial payments aren't accepted.

faqs.q: When does Colorado Springs sell delinquent tax liens?
faqs.a: Every October, online through RealAuction. Overdue taxes are advertised the month before.

faqs.q: Where do I file a Colorado Springs property tax appeal?
faqs.a: Begin with the County Assessor at 1675 West Garden of the Gods Road, Suite 2300. If needed, escalate to the Board of Equalization by July 15.

faqs.q: What happens to a Colorado Springs tax deferral when I sell?
faqs.a: It becomes due on a sale or title transfer. The deferral is recorded as a lien and accrues interest from May 1.
